content.text: Why are spacecraft that are placed into orbit around the Earth generally launched in an easterly direction?
To gain assistance from the wind
To help slow down the spacecraft so it can go into orbit
To reduce the interference from the Earth's magnetic field
To use the Earth's rotation to increase the spacecraft's speed

The Earth's surface is already moving: a point on the equator travels round with the Earth's rotation at about $460\,\mathrm{m/s}$. A launch that adds to this existing speed needs less speed from the rocket itself.
D
The Earth rotates once in about $24\,\mathrm{h}$, so a point on its surface already has an easterly speed of order $\frac{2\pi r}{T} \approx 460\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Launching towards the east means the spacecraft starts with the Earth's rotational velocity already added to it, so the rocket only has to supply the difference between that and orbital speed. This saves fuel and payload.
Launching westwards would subtract from the Earth's rotation, and the other options (wind, magnetic field, slowing down) play no part in achieving orbit. Option D.

content.text: Wire, axle, armature, commutator and brushes can be used to build a device. Which of the following devices requires ALL of these components?
Transformer
DC generator
Galvanometer
Induction motor
Work through the devices one at a time and ask which ones need a coil that rotates on an axle, together with a split-ring or slip-ring contact made through brushes.
B

A DC generator converts mechanical energy into direct current. An armature (coil of wire) is rotated on an axle in a magnetic field, and the emf in the coil reverses every half turn, so a split-ring commutator collects the current through brushes and delivers a unidirectional output.

A transformer has no moving parts, so it needs neither an axle, an armature, a commutator nor brushes. A galvanometer has a small coil on a pivot but no commutator and brushes. An induction motor has a rotor and a stator but no commutator or brushes, since its current is supplied to a stationary stator winding.
Only the DC generator requires all five components. Option B.

content.text: A pendulum is used to determine the value of acceleration due to gravity. The length of the pendulum is varied, and the time taken for the same number of oscillations is recorded. Which of the following could increase the reliability of the results?
Changing the mass of the pendulum
Identifying the independent and dependent variables
Recording all measurements to at least four significant figures
Repeating each measurement several times and recording the average
Reliability is about repeatability: a result is more reliable when the same procedure gives consistent values. Accuracy is about how close a value is to the true value.
Decide which of the four suggestions makes the random scatter in the timing smaller, rather than merely changing the design of the experiment or the number of digits written down.
D

The main random error in timing a pendulum is the reaction time in starting and stopping the timer, which varies from trial to trial. Repeating each measurement several times and taking the average spreads these random errors and gives a more consistent set of results, so the value of $g$ is more reliable.

Changing the mass of the bob changes the design of the experiment, and identifying the independent and dependent variables is good experimental design rather than a change in repeatability. Recording to four significant figures only increases the precision of the written value; it does not remove the scatter in the timings themselves.
Option D.

content.text: Why was germanium used to make the first transistors?
It was an abundant semiconductor.
It was cheaper than other semiconductors.
Its properties allowed for simpler circuit design.
It was easier to purify than other semiconductors.

A transistor only works if the semiconductor's electrical behaviour is very uniform. Think about which property of the raw material, rather than its price or its abundance, was the limiting factor in the late 1940s.
D

Transistor action depends on the majority carriers in a semiconductor being predictable, and impurities introduce unwanted charge carriers that swamp the signal. So the material had to be available in a very pure state.

Of the semiconductors known at the time, germanium could be purified to a much higher degree than the others, so it was used for the first transistors. Silicon has the better properties for a device but its higher melting point made it far harder to purify, and it was not used until the 1950s.
Germanium was not chosen because it was abundant or cheap, and its properties did not simplify circuit design. Option D.

content.text:
Electricity is transported over long distances by transmission lines that are supported by pylons.
How are these transmission lines protected from lightning strikes?
The pylons are insulated from the ground.
There is a grounded wire on top of each pylon.
The transmission lines carry voltages similar to that of lightning.
Large ceramic insulators separate the transmission lines from the pylons.
A lightning strike follows the easiest conducting path to earth. Ask what is deliberately placed at the top of the pylon to provide that path, and why the insulators below it must not provide one.
B

An earth (overhead ground) wire is strung above the transmission lines and connected to a low-resistance earth stake, so a strike on or near the pylon is conducted safely to ground without passing through the lines.

The large ceramic insulators deliberately hold each conductor clear of the metal pylon. That keeps the fault current on the earth wire rather than allowing it to arc to the pylon, and it keeps the lines physically isolated from the earth.
Pylons are not insulated from the ground - they are the opposite, being well earthed - and the line voltage bears no relation to the voltage of a lightning discharge. Option B.

content.text:
A satellite is in a high orbit around the Earth. A particle of dust is in the same orbit.
Which row of the table correctly compares their potential energy and orbital speed?
Potential energy different; orbital speed the same.
Potential energy different; orbital speed different.
Potential energy the same; orbital speed the same.
Potential energy the same; orbital speed different.

Both objects are in the same orbit, so they are at the same distance from the Earth's centre. Use $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ to compare their speeds, then use $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ to compare their potential energies.
A

Orbital speed follows from the circular motion condition $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{GMm}{r^2}$, giving $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$. This depends only on the radius of the orbit, not on the mass of the orbiting object.
Since the satellite and the dust particle are in the same orbit, they have the same orbital speed, even though the satellite is many orders of magnitude more massive.

Gravitational potential energy $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ is directly proportional to the mass $m$, so the satellite's potential energy is far more negative than that of the dust particle: the two are different. Option A.

Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that produces it. Decide which way the magnet's field threads the coil as the pole approaches, then which way the induced current must make its own field inside the coil.
Link the direction of the field inside the coil to the direction of the current seen from the top using the right-hand grip rule.

Using the right-hand grip rule, an induced field directed upwards through the coil corresponds to a current that circulates anticlockwise when the coil is viewed from the top. Option B.

content.text: Why is an iron core used in a transformer?
To limit eddy currents
To reduce the heat generated
To separate the magnetic fields
To increase the linkage of the flux
The primary coil produces a changing magnetic field. Ask what the core does to that field, since the emf induced in the secondary depends on how much of the flux links it.
D

The core is a soft, easily magnetised iron that concentrates and guides the magnetic flux produced by the primary coil so that most of it passes through the secondary coil. A larger flux linking the secondary gives a larger induced emf, $|\varepsilon| = N\left|\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$.

Limiting eddy currents and the heat they cause is the job of laminating and insulating the core, not of the iron itself, and a core is used to link flux rather than to separate the two magnetic fields.
Option D.

content.text: The resistance of two identical-looking wires is measured. One of the wires is made of copper and the other is made of a copper alloy. Why does the wire made of the copper alloy have a higher resistance?
The alloy has more impurities than the copper.
There are more holes in the copper than the alloy.
The alloy retains heat more easily than the copper.
There is a greater energy gap between the conduction and valence bands for the alloy.
Resistance depends on how easily the conduction electrons can move through the material. Consider what alloying does to the regular arrangement of atoms in pure copper.
A

In a copper alloy, atoms of other elements are randomly substituted into the copper lattice. These impurity atoms sit at different equilibrium positions and scatter the conduction electrons, reducing their mean free path and drift velocity.

From $R = \rho\frac{L}{A}$ the resistivity $\rho$ of the alloy is therefore greater than that of pure copper, so two wires of the same length and cross-section have $R_{\text{alloy}} > R_{\text{copper}}$.

Holes are not the majority carriers in a metal, heat retention is unrelated to resistance, and a wider gap between the valence and conduction bands would make the alloy an insulator, which an alloyed copper never is - copper retains a partially filled band. Option A.

content.text:
The diagram shows two experiments. In Experiment 1, the magnet is moved away from the coil. In Experiment 2, the coil is moved away from the magnet.
Why is the same electromotive force (emf) produced in both experiments?

content.alt_text: Two side-by-side experiment sketches. In Experiment 1 a bar magnet labelled N faces a coil labelled G, with the magnet moving away at 3 m s-1; in Experiment 2 the coil moves away from the stationary magnet at 3 m s-1. The relative separation changes at the same rate in both.

content.text: Energy is conserved.
The motor effect generates the same force.
The relative motion between the coil and the magnet is the same.
Both the direction of the magnetic field and the direction of the motion change.

The emf depends only on how quickly the magnetic flux linking the coil is changing, $|\varepsilon| = N\left|\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$. Ask which quantity is identical in the two arrangements.
Neither conservation of energy nor the motor effect fixes the size of an induced emf, so the choice has to come from the rate at which the coil and the magnet approach or separate.
C
The flux linking the coil depends on the field of the magnet and the position of the coil relative to it, so only the rate of change of that relative position matters.

In experiment 1 the magnet moves away at $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ with the coil fixed; in experiment 2 the coil moves away at $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ with the magnet fixed. In both cases the separation changes at $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $\left|\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$ - and hence the emf - is the same.
Energy conservation always holds and says nothing about the emf, and the motor effect is the reverse process. Option C.

content.text: Why is there low intensity of black body radiation at very short wavelengths?
The energy of each photon is reduced at very short wavelengths.
There are fewer photons with high energy at very short wavelengths.
Only photons of very short wavelengths are reabsorbed by the black body.
Photons of very short wavelengths interact with each other causing destructive interference.
Compare the energy carried by a short-wavelength photon, $E = hc/\lambda$, with the number of photons present at that wavelength. The graph shows their product, the intensity.
The fall-off at short wavelengths comes from the number of photons collapsing, not from photons losing energy or interfering with one another.
B
In Planck's law the energy of each photon is $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, so photons at very short wavelengths are individually very energetic - the opposite of what would explain a low intensity.

However the number of photons at those wavelengths falls away far more rapidly than their energy increases, so the product of photon energy and photon number - the radiated intensity - is very small. This steep fall is the short-wavelength cutoff of the black body curve.
Nothing reduces the photon energy, and photons of the same frequency do not interfere with each other in the cavity. Option B.

The diagrams show a wire loop rotating anticlockwise in a radial magnetic field and in a parallel magnetic field. There is a constant current in the wire loop.
Which pair of graphs best describes the behaviour of the force ($F$) on the length of wire $PQ$ as a function of time ($t$) for one revolution of the wire loop?

content.alt_text: Two perspective drawings side by side of a square current-carrying wire loop PQ mounted on a shaft between the N and S poles of a magnet and connected to a cell. The left drawing is labelled 'Radial magnetic field' and shows the loop lying in a plane that contains the field lines; the right drawing is labelled 'Parallel magnetic field' and shows the loop lying in a plane perpendicular to the field. Both show a curved arrow about the rotation axis.

Pair of force-time graphs: the left graph, for a radial field, is a sine curve starting at a positive maximum $F$ at $t = 0$, crossing zero and reaching a negative minimum; the right graph, for a parallel field, is also a sine curve starting at a positive maximum $F$ at $t = 0$ and falling to a negative minimum.

Pair of force-time graphs: the left graph, for a radial field, is a square wave that starts at a positive value, switches abruptly to a negative value and back; the right graph, for a parallel field, is a sine curve starting at a positive maximum $F$ at $t = 0$.

Pair of force-time graphs: the left graph, for a radial field, is a square wave that starts at a positive value and switches abruptly to a negative value and back; the right graph, for a parallel field, is also a square wave starting at a positive value and switching abruptly to a negative value and back.

Pair of force-time graphs: the left graph, for a radial field, is a sine curve starting at a positive maximum $F$ at $t = 0$; the right graph, for a parallel field, is a square wave that starts at a positive value and switches abruptly to a negative value and back.

content.text: Use $F = BIl\sin\omega$ for the side PQ: ask, for each of the two field arrangements, whether the angle between the side and the field changes as the loop turns.
In both cases the sign of the force reverses every half turn, so the correct pair cannot be two smoothly varying curves that pass through zero twice in one revolution.
C
The current in the loop is constant, so the force on the side PQ is $F = BIl\sin\omega$, where $\omega$ is the angle between the side and the field.

In the radial field the field lines are arranged so that PQ stays perpendicular to the field throughout the revolution. The magnitude of the force is therefore constant at $F = BIl$, and because the current in the coil reverses every half turn, the force alternates between $+F$ and $-F$: a square wave. This immediately eliminates the options showing a sine curve for the radial field.

In the parallel field the loop is arranged so that PQ is also at right angles to the field as it revolves, so the force is again constant in magnitude and alternating in sign - a second square wave. This eliminates the option with a sine curve for the parallel field, leaving the pair of square waves.
Option C.

content.text: Which of the following is a consequence of the motor effect?
Rapid heating in an induction cooktop
Minimising energy loss in transmission lines
The wire loops of an operating transformer pulling its coils together
A superconductor repelling small magnetic dust particles vertically above it

The motor effect is a force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Check which statement actually describes a current-carrying conductor in a field, rather than heating, transmission efficiency or superconductivity.
C
A consequence of the motor effect must show a force acting on a conductor that is carrying current in a magnetic field.

In a transformer the alternating current in the secondary coil flows in the magnetic field produced by the changing flux from the primary, and the two sets of current-carrying conductors attract each other, so the coils pull together. That is the motor effect at work.

Rapid heating in an induction cooktop is eddy-current heating from electromagnetic induction; minimising energy loss in transmission lines comes from using a high voltage and a low current so that $I^2R$ is small; and a superconductor levitating magnetic dust is the Meissner effect, not a force on a current. Option C.

The generator is rotated by one revolution in the first second with the switch open. It is then rotated by one revolution in the next second with the switch closed.
Which graph shows the current produced by this generator for these two seconds?

Graph of current in amperes against time in seconds: a full sinusoidal cycle occupies the first second (0 to 1 s) and the trace is a flat line on the time axis from 1 s to 2 s.
Graph of current in amperes against time in seconds: the trace is a flat line on the time axis from 0 to 1 s, then a full sinusoidal cycle from 1 s to 2 s (correct option).

content.text: With the switch open the circuit is incomplete, so no current can flow however fast the coil rotates. Then decide what the coil produces during the second, closed-circuit second.
One complete revolution of a coil gives one complete cycle of emf, and nothing about the coil or its rotation changes between the two revolutions.
B
For the first second the switch is open, so the circuit is broken: an emf is induced in the rotating coil, but no current can flow and the trace stays on the time axis.
For the second second the switch is closed and one full revolution completes one cycle of the alternating emf, so the current is a sine curve filling the interval from 1 s to 2 s.

The graph with the alternating current in the first second has the switch states reversed, the two graphs with current throughout both seconds ignore the open switch, and the graph with a smaller second cycle cannot occur because nothing has changed between the two revolutions. Option B.

content.text:
Two masses have a gravitational force of $12\,\mathrm{N}$ between them.
If the distance between the masses is doubled, what would be the new gravitational force between them?
$3\,\mathrm{N}$
$6\,\mathrm{N}$
$12\,\mathrm{N}$
$24\,\mathrm{N}$
Newton's law of universal gravitation is an inverse square law: work out what happens to $r^2$, not just to $r$, when the separation is doubled.
A
The gravitational force between two masses is $F = \frac{GMm_1m_2}{r^2}$, so $F \propto \frac{1}{r^2}$.
Doubling the separation multiplies $r^2$ by $2^{2} = 4$, so the force becomes one quarter of its original value.
Halving the force (rather than quartering it) would result from doubling $r$ in a first-power relation such as $F \propto \frac{1}{r}$, which is not the case here. Option A.

content.text: How did Hertz determine the speed of radio waves?
By measuring the interference pattern of radio waves
By sending radio waves through a block of pitchblende
By balancing the effect of a magnetic field in a cathode ray tube
By comparing the intensity of two perpendicular beams of radio waves
Hertz never timed a pulse travelling from A to B. He made two sets of radio waves interact with each other and read information off the pattern they produced.
The spacing of the interference (standing wave) fringes gives the wavelength of the radio waves, and the frequency was set by his oscillator.
Once you have a wavelength and a frequency, the speed follows from $v = f\lambda$ - so the answer is a statement about a measurement technique, not about a substance or a balance.
A

Hertz drove a spark-gap oscillator that produced radio waves, reflected them back off a metal ring (or a second spark gap) and let the incident and reflected waves interfere. The distance between successive nodes of the standing wave gave the wavelength, and with the known oscillation frequency he obtained $v = f\lambda \approx 3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

The distractors belong to other parts of physics: sending radiation through pitchblende is Becquerel's discovery of radioactivity, and balancing magnetic effects in a cathode ray tube is Thomson's measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron. Comparing the intensities of two perpendicular beams is not a way of finding a speed.

items: 1 mark: selects option A.

The diagram shows an alpha particle and a proton, placed at equal distances from two large charged metal plates.
Which of the following best describes the motion of the particles?

content.text: Both particles move with the same acceleration.
The alpha particle moves with half the acceleration of the proton.
The alpha particle moves with twice the acceleration of the proton.
The alpha particle moves with a quarter of the acceleration of the proton.
Between two large parallel plates the field is uniform, so both particles experience the same field strength $E$, whatever their masses or charges.
Use $F = qE$ for each particle and then $a = \dfrac{F}{m}$. An alpha particle has twice the charge and four times the mass of a proton.
Ratio the two accelerations rather than calculating each one, and remember both particles are positively charged so both are pushed towards the negative plate.
B

The field between the plates points from the positive lower plate to the negative upper plate, so it is directed upward. Both the alpha particle and the proton are positively charged, so each experiences a force $F = qE$ directed upward, and the two are the same distance from the plates.
The accelerations follow from $a = F/m = qE/m$:
An alpha particle is two protons and two neutrons bound together, so its charge is $2e$ and its mass is approximately $4m_p$:

The doubled charge of the alpha particle is cancelled by its fourfold mass, leaving an acceleration of half the proton's. That is the second option; the equal accelerations and the factors of two and four that ignore either the charge or the mass are the traps.

content.text:
The diagram shows a cathode ray entering a magnetic field.
An electric field is applied to cancel the effect of the magnetic field on the cathode ray.
Which row of the table correctly describes the direction of the applied electric field, and the direction of the force acting on the cathode ray as a result of the magnetic field?

content.alt_text: A horizontal arrow labelled 'Cathode ray' travels from left to right into a region marked with a grid of crosses (x) representing a magnetic field directed into the page.

columns: Direction of the electric field applied
Direction of force as result of the magnetic field

content.text: Electric field applied upward; force from the magnetic field upward.
Electric field applied downward; force from the magnetic field upward.
Electric field applied upward; force from the magnetic field downward.
Electric field applied downward; force from the magnetic field downward.
The magnetic force on a moving charge is $F = qvB\sin\theta$. Work out its direction for a *positive* charge first, then remember a cathode ray is a beam of electrons.

To cancel the magnetic force, the electric force on the electron must be equal and opposite. Since $F = qE$ and the charge is negative, the field direction is opposite to the electric force it produces.
Check the two directions in the row are consistent with each other before reading off the row letter.
D

The cathode ray travels to the right and the magnetic field is directed into the page, so the velocity and the field are perpendicular and $\sin\theta = 1$. For a positive charge, $\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$ with $\mathbf{v}$ to the right and $\mathbf{B}$ into the page gives a force directed upward, by the right hand rule.
Cathode rays are electrons, so the charge is negative and the force is reversed: the magnetic field pushes the cathode ray downwards.
The cancelling electric force on the electron must therefore be upwards. From $F = qE$ with $q$ negative, a force upwards requires the electric field to be directed downwards.
The row with an electric field directed downwards and a magnetic force directed downwards is the fourth row, which is the only self-consistent pairing.

content.text:
The rest length of a train is $200\,\mathrm{m}$ and the rest length of a railway platform is $160\,\mathrm{m}$. The train rushes past the platform so fast that, when observed in the platform's frame of reference, the train and the platform are the same length.
How fast is the train moving?
Only the train is moving as far as the observer on the platform is concerned, so only the train's length is length-contracted. The platform's 160 m is measured in its own rest frame.
Use $L = L_0\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}$ with $L_0 = 200\,\mathrm{m}$ for the train and $L = 160\,\mathrm{m}$ for the length that was measured, then solve for $v/c$.
Sanity check: the train is contracted, so it is travelling slower than $c$, and a faster train would appear shorter still.
A

A ball is launched horizontally from a cliff with an initial velocity of $u\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. After two seconds, the ball's velocity is in the direction $45^\circ$ from the horizontal.

content.text: How does the re-entry angle affect the safety of astronauts returning to Earth in a spacecraft?
Consider both extremes of the angle: what happens if the spacecraft comes in very steeply, and what happens if it comes in very shallowly?

If the angle is too steep the spacecraft decelerates too quickly and heats; if too shallow it may be reflected off the atmosphere into space. The safe range is $5.2^\circ$ to $7.2^\circ$.

The angle of re-entry is between $5.2^\circ$ and $7.2^\circ$. If the angle of re-entry is too steep, the spacecraft will decelerate too quickly. Heat will not be able to be dissipated quickly, and hence the spacecraft may be destroyed or cause high g-forces to be experienced. To overcome the high g-forces, astronauts are seated in such a way as to ensure blood is not forced away from the brain. In addition, to ensure a safe landing, parachutes are used to slow the spacecraft enough so the impact with the ground is within safe limits. If the angle is too shallow then there is a concern that the spacecraft will be reflected off the atmosphere into space.

content.text: Explain how the motor effect is used in an AC motor.
Begin by stating what the motor effect is: a force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, with magnitude $F = BIl\sin\theta$.
Then consider the two sides of the rotor coil: their currents run in opposite directions, so the two forces form a couple, and the torque from that couple is what turns the coil.
Finally explain why the coil does not simply swing back when it reaches the opposite position. Think about what the alternating supply does to the currents in the two sides.
Forces on the sides of the rotor coil produce a torque; the alternating current reverses every $180^\circ$ so the torque acts in the same sense.

The motor effect is the production of a force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. In an AC motor the force on the sides of a coil on the rotor produces a torque that causes the coil to rotate. The direction of the torque is maintained in the same sense by the AC applied reversing the current every $180^\circ$ of the coil's rotation. This keeps the motor rotating due to the torque produced by the motor effect.

content.text: How does doping affect the way a current is carried in a semiconductor?
Begin with the undoped semiconductor. Identify which two types of charge carrier carry the current, and explain why there are equal numbers of each.
Then consider doping. Ask what an extra Group V atom contributes to the lattice, and what is missing when a Group III atom is put into the lattice.
Finish by naming the dominant carrier in each doped material and by explaining how doping makes the doped semiconductor a far better conductor than the pure one.
Doping greatly increases conductivity: a Group V impurity gives an n-type semiconductor in which electrons dominate, while a Group III impurity gives a p-type semiconductor in which holes dominate.

Undoped semiconductors have limited conductivity with the valence band and conduction bands separated by a small energy gap. Equal numbers of holes and electrons move in opposite directions to make up the current flow. When an electron jumps into the conduction band it leaves a vacancy, a hole, which is then filled by another electron. Electrons will tend to migrate to the positive side and holes to the negative side creating the current.

The conductivity of the semiconductor can be increased by doping, if either Group III or Group V impurity is added to the semiconductor. Group V impurities add an extra electron to the lattice structure forming an n-type semiconductor. These electrons have a smaller energy gap and electrons become the dominant charge carriers. If a Group III impurity is added a hole is introduced into the lattice structure. Holes are then the dominant charge carriers.

content.text: Explain how the resulting motion of the cannonballs supports Galileo's analysis of projectile motion.
Compare the vertical motions first: the balls reach the same height in the same time, which tells you what their initial vertical velocities have in common.

Reference both of Galileo's claims explicitly: the horizontal component is constant, and the resulting path is a parabola.
Both balls rise and fall in the same vertical way, so the vertical motion is independent of the horizontal component; the horizontal motion is uniform.

Galileo used geometry to show that the trajectory of a projectile is a parabola. The shape of the curve generated is parabolic. He also stated that the horizontal and vertical components of velocity were independent of each other. He also showed that the horizontal component (ignoring resistance) is constant. content.text: Explain how the adoption of AC as the dominant electricity supply benefits society in terms of the advantages of AC over DC.
Identify the two things AC can do that DC cannot: one involves a transformer, the other involves the machine that generates the electricity.
For the transformer point, connect the ability to change voltage to the current in the transmission line through $P = VI$, and then to the loss in that line through $P = I^{2}R$.

For the generation point, compare the slip rings of an AC generator with the split-ring commutator of a DC generator at high rotational speed, then follow the consequences for reliability, cost and where the power stations can be built.

AC can be transformed to different voltages, giving lower energy loss in transmission and safe step-down for use, and AC generators are simpler and more reliable at high speed; this makes cheap, reliable power available over long distances.

AC has many advantages over DC in both production and distribution. AC is easy to convert using transformers to different voltages for different applications. There is less energy loss in high voltage transmissions and hence it can be transmitted over long distances at high voltages and can also be stepped down for usage and safety reasons. This allows power to be generated away from cities and reduces pollution generated in cities. DC cannot be transformed easily so there is a need for DC to be generated close to the source. The cost of DC generation and distribution is higher. Another problem with producing DC is split ring commutators which present problems when running at high speeds. The slip ring commutators of AC are smoother with less arcing. They provide fewer problems and are more reliable. AC allows for the mass production of electricity away from cities and provides a cheap, reliable and flexible power supply which is available throughout much of the modern world today. It has contributed greatly to industrial development creating many goods and services at an affordable price that have allowed our lives to be much easier. Electric refrigerators and washing machines for instance reduce the household chores creating more leisure time. Products such as TV and mobile phones provide information quickly around the world and have contributed to globalisation.

content.text: Earth's magnetic field and sea-floor spreading

(i) Before you draw anything, recall the convention that fixes which way the lines go: field lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole, and the north-seeking end of a compass points along the field. Get this right first or the drawing is wrong everywhere.

(ii) The evidence for sea-floor spreading is written into the rock itself: new basalt forms at the ridge and is magnetised with whatever direction the field happens to have at that moment, so reversals are recorded as stripes.

Then say what the pattern must look like on each side of the ridge - the stripes should mirror one another - and what the ages of the stripes, found by dating the rock, tell you about the rate and direction of spreading.

items: (i) A labelled diagram of a field that is broadly dipolar but inclined to the axis of rotation: field lines enter the Earth near the geographic North Pole, which therefore behaves as a magnetic south pole and attracts the north pole of a compass; they loop out through space and emerge again near the geographic South Pole, running near the surface roughly parallel to the equator and roughly parallel to one another rather than radiating from a point.

(ii) As new basalt forms at a diverging boundary it is magnetised with the direction Earth's field has at that moment, so every polarity reversal is recorded as a parallel stripe of reversed rock. Successive stripes are symmetric about the ridge and get older with distance from it. New crust is therefore being created at the ridge and moving away on both sides at the same rate, which is the evidence for sea-floor spreading.

content.text: (i) Earth's field is close to dipolar but tilted roughly $11^{\circ}$ to the axis of rotation, so it cannot be drawn as a bar magnet lying exactly along that axis. The convention is that field lines leave a north magnetic pole and enter a south magnetic pole; because the north-seeking end of a compass is deflected towards the geographic North Pole, that region behaves as a magnetic south pole. The lines therefore emerge from the southern hemisphere, loop through space and enter near the geographic North Pole, and near the surface they run roughly parallel to the equator and to one another. A good drawing shows a handful of closed loops, all in the same sense, tilted with the axis, with the field direction arrows pointing from south to north along the surface.

(ii) At a diverging plate boundary magma rises and solidifies into new basalt. As it cools through the Curie temperature the iron minerals in it align with whatever direction Earth's field has at that moment and are locked in, so each band of crust records the field direction at the time it formed. Because the field has reversed many times, the ocean floor is divided into parallel bands of alternating polarity, and because the crust is created at the ridge and carried away on both sides, the bands are mirror images of one another about the axis of the ridge. Dating each band shows that the bands become older with increasing distance from the ridge, at a constant rate on each side. The symmetry and the regular age progression are therefore direct evidence that new crust is formed at the ridge and spreads away from it - the mechanism of sea-floor spreading.

content.text: Light, surfaces and remote sensing
What happens to white light when it hits a red surface?
(i) White light is a mixture of wavelengths. Ask what happens to each wavelength at a surface that looks red, and where the energy of the absorbed wavelengths goes.

(ii) Remote sensing measures the spectrum of radiation arriving from the ground, so the question is which parts of that spectrum change when the vegetation does, and why different plants or different damage change the spectrum differently.
Then think about why a single survey is not enough: a change can only be detected by comparing surveys of the same ground taken at different times, so resolution and repeat coverage are both needed.

White light is a mixture of wavelengths. When it hits a red surface the shorter wavelengths are absorbed by the surface and the longer wavelengths, such as red light, are reflected to the observer, so the surface appears red.

White light arriving at a surface is a superposition of wavelengths, and the interaction with the material is wavelength-dependent: photons of some wavelengths are absorbed and raise the internal energy of the surface, while photons of the remaining wavelengths are reflected or scattered back out. Because the pigment in a red surface reflects the long wavelengths and absorbs the short ones, the light leaving the surface is dominated by red, so the surface appears red. The energy balance is that the reflected light carries away only the wavelengths that were not absorbed, and the absorbed fraction becomes heat.

content.text: Light, surfaces and remote sensing
Describe how remote sensing can be used to monitor changes in vegetation.

A satellite records the spectrum of radiation arriving from the Earth's surface in several bands. Healthy vegetation has a characteristic reflectance signature: chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the blue and red so the visible reflectance is low, while the internal cell structure reflects strongly in the near infrared. That signature changes with species, growth stage, moisture stress, drought, fire damage and clearing, so repeated surveys of the same ground from the same sensor are compared and the change in the band ratios (a vegetation index) is mapped. The method is passive, covers very large areas repeatedly and cheaply, is non-destructive, and is repeated often enough to follow a growing season.

Remote sensing works because every surface has a characteristic reflectance and emission spectrum. Leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs in the blue and red and reflects in the green, and they are bright in the near infrared because the internal cell structure scatters that radiation strongly. Both features are sensitive to the state of the plant: species, growth stage, chlorophyll content, water stress and damage by drought or bushfire all change the reflectance in individual bands. An orbiting sensor therefore produces an image of each band for the whole scene, and a vegetation index or band ratio computed from those images maps the vegetation type. Repeated acquisitions of the same ground allow image differencing, so a change such as clearing, fire or drought is detected as a change in the index, without disturbing the site and at a coverage and revisit rate that a ground survey could not match.

content.text: Compare the use of seismic refraction and seismic reflection techniques in oil and gas exploration.
Both techniques send a wave into the ground and detect it at the surface with geophones, so start by listing what they share before you look for differences.

They differ in which part of the arriving signal they use: one exploits the very first arrivals, the other exploits later echoes from a boundary. Ask which kind of boundary and which depth each one images best.

Then say what an oil or gas reservoir looks like in the resulting data - you are looking for an anomaly against the background rather than a uniform layer, and you should say which way the anomaly appears.

Reflection surveys map deep interfaces and are the main technique for locating oil and gas reservoirs, while refraction surveys use first arrivals and are generally used for shallow targets; both send waves through Earth and detect them with geophones.

All seismic surveys use an energy source to send waves through Earth. These waves are reflected or refracted off the interface caused by rocks with different densities. The waves reach the surface and are detected with geophones. In reflection surveys, the waves are reflected off the interfaces and multichannel seismographs can be used to map several horizons with each shot. Seismic refraction surveys use first arrivals that are refracted along the interfaces and are generally used for shallow targets. Seismic data is used to interpret subsurface geology such as reefs and anticlines.

In oil and gas exploration reservoirs generally have different properties and are shown as anomalies on seismic traces. For example, bright spots may indicate gas accumulations and oil interfaces may show up as flat surfaces.

content.text: Survey data
With reference to the diagram and the table, explain why data reduction has to be carried out on the raw data from this survey before geologists can assess the potential resource.

Work out from the table what else, apart from the resource, could be setting the gravimeter readings. Look for columns that vary from station to station - altitude is the obvious one, and so is the substrate.

A free-air correction removes the change in $g$ caused simply by being higher or lower off a datum. A Bouguer correction then removes the effect of the extra rock between the station and the datum. You need both here because the stations span a range of altitudes on the flank of a hill.

Remember too that the Bouguer correction assumes a density for the rock above the datum, so the differing densities of sandstone and granite have to be accounted for, and that the nearby topography (Mount Noble) also needs correcting. Only what is left after all of this is a candidate anomaly.

The stations are at different altitudes near a hill, and the readings are affected by altitude, nearby topography and the differing densities of sandstone and granite, so free-air, altitude and Bouguer corrections must be applied.

Raw gravity values above a resource will reflect the nature of the resource including size, shape and density of the component rocks as well as properties of nearby features. Data reduction is the processing of the raw data to remove the components of gravity not related to the resource.

The gravity stations are at different altitudes and there is a high hill, Mount Noble, close by. A free air correction should be made to eliminate decreases in gravity due to distance from the centre of Earth. An altitude correction should be made to remove increased gravity because of the increased thickness of rock at higher altitude. A Bouguer correction should be made to resolve the difference between the expected value and the actual value. The differences in probable rock densities have to be taken into account as sandstone is likely to be less dense than granite.

content.text: Explain how geophysical methods have benefited mineral exploration programs.

Make the general point first: geophysics looks for a physical signature of the target - a density contrast, a magnetic contrast, a radioactivity contrast, a seismic velocity contrast - and that signature is what makes the deposit findable without digging.

Then make the practical point: once the instrument can be carried on an aircraft, the survey rate rises by orders of magnitude and the cost per unit area falls, so a far larger area can be covered for the same money.

Finish by connecting both to exploration programs: many more targets are screened cheaply before drilling, so fewer dry holes are drilled and the success rate of the program rises. That is the benefit the question is asking you to justify.
Airborne gravity, magnetic and radiometric surveys cover very large areas quickly and cheaply, so many more targets can be identified and screened before expensive drilling, raising success rates.

Geophysics is the analysis of features of Earth using data other than direct measurement. Early mineral exploration programs relied on surface observations of rocks which were compiled into maps from which subsurface features were interpreted. Geophysical methods use the laws of physics to interpret the features of Earth. For example, some mineral deposits have a magnetic signature which shows up as a magnetic anomaly which can be drilled; large or very dense ore bodies have a gravity anomaly; some ores contain radioactive elements which show up as a radiometric anomaly; seismic surveys can be used to determine geological structures, and the shape and depth of basins.

Geophysical surveys can be readily adapted to modern transport methods such as airborne surveys using helicopters. Airborne radiometric and magnetic surveys can cover very large areas and acquire very large amounts of data in a short time. A land gravity survey may take many days whereas the same survey can be carried out using a helicopter in a day. Thus the surveys are cheaper. Remote sensing techniques can be used to rapidly manipulate and process data thus making it cheaper to interpret the data.

Because of the speed at which large volumes of data can be interpreted, larger areas can be covered and more potential targets identified and evaluated for drilling. Less productive targets can be eliminated thus increasing success rates.

content.text: Ultrasound and medical imaging
Part (i) is about blood, which is moving. Ask what happens to the frequency of a wave that is reflected from a moving scatterer, and what the size of that change tells you about the motion.

Part (ii) is about the scan shown. Read it as echo strength against time: it is a one-dimensional record. Think about what a computer has to do with many such records before a two-dimensional picture exists.

For part (i) you need three things: the name of the effect, the cause of the frequency change, and the quantity that the change measures. For part (ii) the key idea is that the image is assembled, not that a single scan produces it.

items: (i) The Doppler effect. Because the blood cells are moving along the beam, the reflected ultrasound is frequency shifted, and the difference between the transmitted and reflected frequencies measures the blood flow.

(ii) The scan is repeated at many positions or angles over the same area; each is converted into a B scan and the B scans are analysed and overlaid by a computer to build a two-dimensional image of the internal structures.

content.text: Part (i). Ultrasound is reflected at the boundary between the blood and the surrounding tissue. Because the blood cells are moving towards or away from the transducer, the reflected wave is Doppler shifted. For a scatterer moving at speed $v$ along the beam the exact shift is $f' = f\dfrac{c + v}{c - v}$, which for $v \ll c$ becomes $f' \approx f\left(1 + \dfrac{2v}{c}\right)$. The difference between the transmitted frequency and the reflected frequency is therefore proportional to the component of the blood velocity along the beam, so measuring that difference gives the flow.

Part (ii). The single trace shown is an A scan: echo strength plotted against time, with a peak at each interface. A computer converts each A scan into a B scan, in which echo strength is plotted against position along the beam rather than against time, which gives the depth of each interface. Sweeping the transducer so that many adjacent or oblique beam lines are recorded, and displaying them side by side, builds up a two-dimensional image of the internal structure.

content.text: X-ray radiation and CT scanning
Part (i) is an X-ray tube. One component supplies the electrons, a second stops them, and a third controls where the radiation leaves. Ask which part of the electron's energy becomes the X-rays.
Part (ii) is a comparison, so build a two-column list: what each technique can resolve, and what each one needs from the tissues it images. Lung tissue is the awkward case - ask why.
Remember a CT scan does not use a different radiation source. It changes what is done with the information after the radiation has passed through the patient.

items: (i) A heated tungsten filament releases electrons, which are accelerated by a high potential difference onto a tungsten target. Most of their kinetic energy becomes heat, but a small fraction is converted into X-radiation, which is directed out through a window.

(ii) A CT scan has a higher resolution than a conventional X-ray and produces a three-dimensional image of the interior of the lung, whereas a conventional X-ray needs high contrast between body structures, which lung tissue does not provide, so its result may not be good enough for a diagnosis.

content.text: Part (i). The filament is heated so that it emits electrons by thermionic emission. A high potential difference between the filament and the anode accelerates the electrons so that they strike the tungsten target with high kinetic energy. On impact the electrons are stopped, and almost all of their energy is converted into thermal energy which is removed by cooling the anode. A small fraction is converted into X-radiation, which is emitted from the focus of the target and leaves the tube through a window, after passing through filters that shape the beam and a collimator that limits the area being imaged.

Part (ii). A conventional radiograph is a single projection, so structures at different depths are superimposed and the only contrast available is the difference in X-ray absorption between the tissues. Lung tissue is mostly air, so it absorbs X-rays only slightly more than the air around it and very little contrast is produced; a small tumour can therefore be missed altogether. A CT scan acquires many projections over a range of angles, and a computer reconstructs them into cross-sectional slices, which can be combined into a three-dimensional image. The CT scan therefore resolves the low-contrast lung tissue far better and also shows the depth of any lesion.

content.text: Describe how this transmutation is used to produce a diagnostic image.

Identify the particle in the equation first: ${}^{0}_{+1}\mathrm{e}$ is a positron, and the equation shows carbon-11 decaying by positron emission. Ask what happens when a positron meets an electron inside the body, and what happens to the energy.

Two photons are produced at that event. Momentum has to be conserved, so think about the directions in which the two photons can leave the site, and about how a ring of detectors arranged around the patient could use that to work out where the event happened.

Do not forget the delivery side of the technique: something is administered to the patient before the scan, and it does not spread evenly. Ask why it ends up concentrated in the tissue being investigated.
A positron emitted by the radiopharmaceutical annihilates with an electron, producing two gamma rays emitted 180 degrees apart which are detected in coincidence to locate the emitting region.

A positron emission tomography (PET) device uses a radioisotope that is deficient in neutrons. During decay radioisotopes such as Carbon-11 protons decay to produce neutrons and positrons. Positrons are positively charged electrons. At the beginning of a procedure a radiopharmaceutical which contains the radioisotope is given to the patient with the radioisotope accumulating in the area of the body under investigation. During the short decay period an emitted positron interacts with an electron where the radiopharmaceutical has accumulated, annihilating each other to produce two gamma rays which are emitted at 180 degrees to each other. These gamma rays are detected by sensors surrounding the body called photomultipliers and converted to an electrical signal. The electrical signal is amplified and applied to a computer which constructs an image based on the location of the gamma ray pairs.

content.text: Describe how properties of protons in nuclei are used in the production of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
Begin with the property of the proton that allows it to interact with a magnetic field at all, and with what happens to that interaction when a very strong, uniform external field is applied.

Then ask about the frequency of the resulting motion, and about what has to be applied to the protons if energy is to be transferred to them efficiently. The keyword here is resonance, and the frequency of the applied pulse has to match the frequency of the protons.

Finally, consider what the protons do immediately after the pulse stops, and how that behaviour is picked up and turned into an image. The full chain field, alignment, pulse, relaxation, detection, image is what the top mark is for.

Protons have nuclear spin; in a strong field they align and precess at a frequency set by the field. A matching RF pulse tips them, and the radio waves emitted as they relax are detected and processed into an image.

Protons in nuclei carry a magnetic spin which can couple to an external field. When protons in nuclei are subjected to a strong uniform external field their two spin orientations align at an angle with the external field, tracing out a conical path centred around the direction of the external field. This process is called precession. The frequency of the precession motion of spins depends on the external field.

A radio frequency (RF) oscillator pulse matching the precession frequency applied to these protons causes aligned spins to flip as well as to precess in step (in phase) with each other, which creates a magnetic field perpendicular to the external field. After the RF pulse some protons flip back to their original state and emit radio waves which can be detected by a radio receiver and processed by a computer to produce an image (MRI).

content.text: Assess the impact of medical applications of physics on society.

This part is an assessment, so plan two sides before you write: the benefits of the applications, and the costs they impose. Then finish with a conclusion that actually weighs the two against each other.

Support each point with a specific named application taken from earlier in the question - X-rays, CT, MRI, ultrasound, radiotherapy or endoscopy - rather than making a general claim about medicine. A general claim earns no marks here.

Read the top band of the marking criteria before you start: it asks for positive and negative effects both clearly related to the applications, an informed judgement, and organised use of appropriate terminology.
Non-invasive diagnosis has improved health outcomes and reduced mortality, but has raised costs, strained health budgets and created ethical dilemmas about information that cannot yet be treated.

Medical technology has benefited from the wider advances in physics with the invention of X-rays, computer-aided tomography (CAT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, radiotherapy and endoscopy for use in medical diagnosis. All of these tools are widely available non-invasive diagnostic procedures.

The use of non-invasive medical technology enables simpler medical procedures to be performed which do not require hospitalisation or surgery to obtain information or can provide diagnostic information where an invasive procedure is not possible eg foetal ultrasound. In addition, the possibility of infection is eliminated in a non-invasive diagnostic investigation. Further, with the widespread availability of non-invasive diagnostic procedures the general health of people has improved, mortality rate has been reduced, life expectancy is longer.

However, this has come at a cost. The costs of medical technology, aged care and the availability of expensive diagnostic investigation have pushed up the price of health beyond what individuals can afford and places great strain on the economic ability of a nation to provide affordable health care to all its citizens.

Advances in non-invasive medical technology and their use can collide with the morals and ethical principles of the society or provide diagnostic information which is beyond safe treatment eg brain tumours or foetal abnormalities. This has the potential to delay or prohibit new technology and treatments from becoming quickly available to the detriment of people who would benefit.
Overall, the advancement of medical technology has been beneficial to society even though the cost is becoming prohibitive.

content.text: Spectral class and coloured filters

Part (i): a filter is a coloured material that transmits strongly in its own band and absorbs most of the rest. Work out which part of the spectrum a class A star emits most of, then what each filter passes and how much.
Part (ii): think about why an astronomer would not trust a brightness measured with an arbitrary filter, and then about what you get if the same star is measured through two agreed standard filters.
Part (ii) has two distinct ideas to earn its three marks: making measurements comparable, and getting a new quantity out of the comparison. Name both.

items: (i) A class A star emits more blue light than red. A blue filter transmits only the blue light, so more of the star's light reaches the observer and it appears brighter; a red filter transmits only the small amount of red light that the star emits, so the star appears dimmer.

(ii) A standard set of filters makes the brightness measurement reproducible between stars and between observatories, and the ratio of the brightness measured through two filters - the colour index - is a quantitative measure of the star's colour that can be used to classify it.

content.text: Part (i). Class A stars are hotter than the Sun, so by Wien's law their spectrum peaks at a shorter wavelength, in the blue. A coloured filter transmits strongly only within its own narrow band and absorbs most of the rest of the spectrum, so the light reaching the eye is dominated by the band the filter passes. Through the blue filter the observer receives a large fraction of the star's total output, whereas through the red filter, which passes only the weak long-wavelength tail of the spectrum, much less light gets through. The star therefore appears brighter through the blue filter.

Part (ii). The brightness recorded from a star depends on which filter was used, so a measurement taken with an arbitrary filter is not reproducible and cannot be compared with anyone else's result. Adopting a standard set of filters, for example the blue (B) and yellow-green (V) astronomical systems, fixes the bands used and standardises the measurement. Because the ratio of the two recorded intensities, $m_B - m_V$, depends only on the shape of the star's spectrum and not on its overall brightness, it is a quantitative measure of colour. This colour index can be used to assign a temperature and a spectral class to the star, and to compare stars observed with different instruments.

content.text: An astronomer has noticed that a star has become brighter. Explain TWO possible reasons for the change in brightness.
The question asks for TWO explanations, so have two ready and make each one a real explanation rather than just a name. Each is worth about two marks.

The graph of apparent magnitude against time is the clue for one of them. Ask whether the change is a one-off or whether it repeats, and over what time scale - and what physical process in a star would produce each pattern.

For the other, ask what happens to a very massive star when it runs out of fuel, and then ask how long such an event would take compared with a few days. The timescale is what tells the two explanations apart.

Either a supernova (an extreme, sudden, temporary brightening caused by a rapidly expanding shell) or a Cepheid variable, which shows a distinctive repeating light curve over days or weeks as the star expands and contracts.
The change in brightness could be due to a supernova if the change in brightness is extreme, sudden and temporary. This is due to the rapidly expanding shell.

Another reason could be that the star was a Cepheid variable. If it was a Cepheid, one would expect to observe a distinctive light curve, increases and decreases in intensity, over a period of a few days or weeks. This is due to the expansion and contraction of the star.

content.text: Explain how this data provides evidence for the evolutionary age of the stars in this cluster.
Two independent pieces of evidence are given - the H-R diagram and the two spectra - and both have to be explained. Treat them as two separate arguments.

On the diagram, the most telling feature for an old cluster is what is missing from the main sequence rather than what is present. Look for the point at which the sequence of plotted stars turns away from the sequence, and relate that to the lifetime of a star of that mass.

For the spectra, compare the widths of the lines in P and Q. Line width is a diagnostic, so ask what a larger width tells you about the density of the gas producing the lines, and therefore about whether that star has expanded.

There are no hot blue main sequence stars, so the cluster's turn-off is at class G; the Sun takes about 10 billion years, so the cluster is about that old. The broadened spectral lines of Q indicate an expanded red giant.

In a cluster of stars, it is assumed that all of the stars are the same age as they form together. Stars evolve when they run out of fuel. The brighter stars are larger, the mass luminosity relationship shown provides evidence for this. The larger stars 'burn' faster as shown and hence remain on the main sequence for a shorter amount of time. In this cluster, there are no hot blue main sequence stars. The line on the H-R diagram with no dots shows where the larger main sequence stars should have been. This provides evidence for the age of the stars in the cluster as presumably the stars such as the blue stars have evolved into red giants and then white dwarfs. By looking at where the stars turn off the main sequence the age of the star can be predicted. In this cluster the turn off point is for stars of G class or stars similar to our Sun. The Sun is expected to live for about 10 billion years. The cluster is hence about 10 billion years old.

The evidence for their evolution can be found in their position on the H-R diagram eg a red giant is brighter than a red main sequence star. As they are the same colour it is assumed they are the same temperature. Looking at the spectra more carefully it can be seen that the spectral lines are narrower indicating that the star itself is less dense than a main sequence star, providing evidence that the star expanded as part of its evolutionary process.

content.text: Evaluate methods of obtaining good quality images of celestial objects using ground-based telescopes.
This is an evaluation, and the marks come from pairing each method with both its benefit and its cost, then reaching a judgement. A list of methods on its own will not score highly here.

Start by listing the problems: the atmosphere distorts and absorbs light, a large mirror deforms under its own weight, and faint objects are difficult to detect. Every method you name should be matched to one of these problems.

Note that more than one corrective optical technique is available and that they operate at very different rates. Ask yourself whether the fast techniques and the slow techniques suffer from the same drawbacks - that comparison is where the judgement in this part comes from.

No single method solves every problem: high, remote sites and active optics help with mirror distortion, while adaptive optics corrects the atmosphere quickly but with some loss of sensitivity; together they rival space telescopes far more cheaply.

In order to obtain good quality images various problems need to be overcome. No one method seems to address all of the problems. Problems include: the distortion and absorption of light due to the atmosphere; the distortion of the telescope mirror especially as they get bigger; the difficulty in gathering light from faint objects, the background light due to population centres. By initially placing the telescope away from population centres and at high altitude the amount of atmosphere the light has to penetrate is reduced, limiting the problem but not eliminating it. The best locations still have limited resolution for optical telescopes. Further techniques such as active optics can be used to straighten the primary mirrors using actuators and a slow feedback system. This is effective and allows for large mirrors for example 10 m mirrors to be used and sharper images and detection of fainter objects to be created, but the change in the mirror is quite slow. Adaptive optics uses a small flexible mirror to sample and correct the starlight collected by the primary mirror. There is a very fast feedback system and it is very successful in correcting atmospheric distortions but some sensitivity is compromised with this technique. These techniques when combined can form very impressive images at a lower cost than space-based telescopes.

content.text: Photon emission and de Broglie's hypothesis

Part (i): the transition is from $n = 3$ down to $n = 1$. Set $n_i$ and $n_f$ carefully, because it is easy to reverse them. Either the Rydberg equation $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$ or the energy-level route $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}$ followed by $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$ will give the answer.

Part (ii): use de Broglie's hypothesis to picture each allowed electron orbit as a standing wave fitted around the nucleus. Ask what wavelengths those standing waves can have relative to the ground state, and then ask what a photon must match in order to be absorbed.
The key idea in part (ii) is that absorption requires an exact match to a permitted energy difference, and that the ground state is the lowest state so nothing can be absorbed out of it. State both.

items: $\lambda = 1.027\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m} = 102.7\,\mathrm{nm}$, in the ultraviolet.

The electron in the ground state occupies the shortest allowed standing wave. Absorption is only possible if the photon's energy exactly equals the difference between two stationary states, which is always a whole number of ground-state energy quanta. A photon of any other energy corresponds to no permitted transition, and the atom cannot lose energy from the ground state, so the photon is not absorbed.

The wavelength follows from $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$:

This lies in the ultraviolet, which is why hydrogen atoms in a classroom discharge tube glow red (the Balmer lines to $n = 2$) and do not show this line at all. The equivalent Rydberg route $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{1^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{3^{2}}\right)$ with $R = 1.097\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$ gives the same wavelength to three significant figures.

Part (ii). de Broglie's hypothesis treats the electron as a wave as well as a particle, so an electron in a stationary state is a standing wave fitted around the nucleus. The boundary condition permits only a whole number of half-wavelengths in an orbit, so the ground state $n = 1$ has the longest allowed standing wave and each excited state has a shorter one. The allowed energies are therefore quantised, and the spacing between adjacent states decreases as $n$ increases.

A photon can only be absorbed if its energy exactly matches the difference between two permitted states. The ground state is the lowest possible state, so no absorption can take the atom below it, and a photon of any other energy corresponds to no allowed transition. The photon is therefore not absorbed and passes through the atom unchanged.

content.text: Nuclear forces and binding energy

Part (i): compare the two forces acting between the nucleons - gravity and the electrostatic repulsion between protons. Ask which is stronger by how many orders of magnitude, and then ask what must therefore be present to hold the nucleus together at all.

Part (ii): the diagram is binding energy per nucleon against atomic number. Find where the curve is steepest and where it reaches its maximum, then use those two features to decide in which direction energy is released when light nuclei combine and when heavy nuclei split.
Part (ii) also needs the link back to mass-energy equivalence: a change in total binding energy is a change in mass, so say how the released energy is accounted for.

items: The gravitational attraction between nucleons is negligible compared with the electrostatic repulsion between protons, so gravity cannot account for nuclear stability; a much stronger force, the strong nuclear force, must hold the nucleus together.

Fusing light nuclei (below iron) or splitting heavy nuclei (above iron) both raise the average binding energy per nucleon, and the increase in total binding energy is released as energy - fusion and fission. This is consistent with the mass defect, since $E = mc^2$.

content.text: Part (i). Newton's law of universal gravitation does act between the nucleons, but the gravitational force between two nucleons is of order $10^{36}$ times smaller than the electrostatic repulsion between two protons. The nucleus contains many protons, so if gravity were the only attractive force the nucleus would fly apart; it does not, and the repulsion is overwhelming. A third interaction must therefore be at work, and it must be enormously stronger: the strong nuclear force, which acts only over distances of about $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$.

Part (ii). Binding energy per nucleon measures how strongly each nucleon is held in the nucleus. By $E = mc^2$ that binding energy is equal to the mass defect that had to be supplied to build the nucleus, so a nucleus with a higher total binding energy is a lower-mass, lower-energy state.

The curve rises steeply from hydrogen through helium to a maximum of about $8.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon near iron, then falls slowly towards uranium. Fusing nuclei lighter than iron moves the product up the rising part of the curve, so the total binding energy of the product exceeds that of the reactants and the difference is released; this is fusion. Splitting a nucleus heavier than iron into two lighter fragments also moves the products up the curve, so energy is released again; this is fission.
Both are consistent with conservation of mass-energy: because the products are more tightly bound they have slightly less mass, and the missing mass appears as kinetic energy of the products.

content.text: With reference to the properties of neutrons, describe the use of the neutron as a probe.
Build the answer property by property. The neutron is uncharged, and its mass is comparable to a proton's. Ask what each of those lets a neutron do that a charged particle cannot.
For each property, name a concrete use: scanning something you cannot see into, making a particular isotope, or studying structure at the atomic scale.
The question says 'with reference to the properties of neutrons', so every use you list has to be tied back to a property in the same sentence, or it will not earn the marks.

Being neutral and of mass similar to a proton, neutrons penetrate dense, highly charged material and are absorbed only by nuclei, making them useful for imaging and for activating nuclei to make isotopes and to split uranium.

The neutron is a nucleon with a similar mass to the proton. Unlike the proton the neutron has no charge. Hence it is not affected by magnetic or electric field and will not be deflected by the protons in the nucleus allowing the neutron to penetrate dense materials, such as aircraft engines and weld joints. Any interaction with the nucleus, where the neutron is absorbed, is likely to make the nucleus unstable producing isotopes of the element which can be studied for additional properties.

The neutron has properties that are associated with quantum physics. The neutron has a de Broglie wavelength allowing it to interact with materials at the atomic level. This is useful when studying the properties of semiconductors in the production of integrated circuits. If the wavelength is comparable with the inter-atomic lattice spacing then an interference pattern will result which can be analysed. This is useful in the study of biological substances or inorganic substances such as pharmaceuticals.

Slow thermal neutrons produced in a nuclear reactor have energy that is similar to the energy of atomic vibrations in solids and liquids and hence are useful in analysing other properties of atoms. Slow thermal neutrons are also used in a controlled fission reaction. These neutrons interact with a uranium nucleus, splitting the uranium atom, to produce two smaller atoms plus an additional 3 neutrons plus energy.

content.text: Describe the significance of the Manhattan Project to society.
This is a significance question, so you need consequences rather than a description of the project. Ask what was actually produced and what followed from it.

Organise the consequences into two groups: the military and political, such as the bomb, the arms race and the ever-present risk of nuclear attack, and the peaceful, such as nuclear power and radioisotopes for medicine, agriculture and industry. Include at least one clearly negative consequence, such as a reactor accident.
Finish with a statement that weighs the effects, because a significance question is not complete until the overall importance has been judged.
It developed the atomic bomb, which hastened the end of World War II and began the nuclear arms race, but it also produced nuclear power and radioisotopes for medicine, agriculture and industry.

The Manhattan Project was a top-secret nuclear bomb project. Two different types of nuclear bombs and nuclear fission reactors, including the Fermi reactor, were developed as part of this project. The first use of atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki clearly showed the destructive power of such a weapon and hastened the end of World War II. The fear of this weapon led to the nuclear arms race between the USA and the Soviet Union. After the Soviet Union had proved their nuclear capability in 1949, tension between the two nations increased and continued through to the 1990s. Many other nations also developed nuclear weapons. Even after nuclear weapons reduction programs, there are still large stockpiles of weapons, which makes the possibility of nuclear attack a reality for society. Nuclear reactor development has led to the development of nuclear power plants, which has provided a carbon dioxide free power source for society, currently supplying much of Europe's energy. There have been, however, nuclear accidents such as Fukushima, which have had devastating effects: death, disease and rendering regions uninhabitable. Nuclear power plants can also produce radioactive isotopes which have been used to benefit society in medicine, agriculture and industry. In medicine, radiotherapy is used to target cancer and radioactive tracers can be used to test organ function.

content.text: Assess the effectiveness of the Bohr-Rutherford model of the atom in accounting for experimental observations.
An assessment needs a strength and a limitation, each tied to a feature of the model, and then a judgement about whether the limitations were serious enough to require a new model.

Ask first what the classical Rutherford model predicted for a charged electron orbiting a nucleus, and how Bohr's quantised stationary states answered it. That is the model's biggest success, and you should be able to state why the fix worked.

Then test the model against observations beyond the hydrogen spectrum itself: the relative intensities of the spectral lines, what happens to the lines when the atom is placed in an external magnetic field, and the spectra of atoms larger than hydrogen. Each of these is a test the model has to pass or fail.

It successfully explained the hydrogen spectrum and kept the atom stable through quantised stationary states, but it could not explain relative line intensities, the Zeeman effect or the spectra of larger atoms, so a quantum model was needed.

The Bohr model has a central nucleus surrounded by an orbiting electron, as described by Rutherford. This model predicted that the electron would collapse into the nucleus due to the attraction force between the electron and other protons.

Bohr proposed that electrons existed in stationary states and these states were quantised according to de Broglie's wave-particle duality theory, Planck's quantised energy theory and Pauli's exclusion principle which limited the number of electrons that could be in any stationary state. This ensured that the atom remained stable. The model was supported by data in relation to the spectral lines of hydrogen that had previously been observed by Balmer.

Bohr's model, while effective in describing the hydrogen atom, had limitations when applied to other experimental evidence associated with hydrogen atoms. The model was unable to explain the different relative intensities of spectral lines of hydrogen nor could it explain the effect of magnetic fields as described by Zeeman, now known as the Zeeman Effect. The model did not work when applied to the spectral lines of larger atoms, although had some validity for helium. The implication of this was that a new model of the atom was required, one that would be dependent on quantum physics and not the classical model of Bohr and Rutherford.
