content.text: Logic circuits and transducers

Part (i): work along each branch of the circuit from the inputs, remembering what a NOT gate does, and evaluate both outputs for all four input combinations. The wire crossings shown with a small hump do not connect, which changes which input reaches which gate.

Part (ii): write the definition of an input transducer and the definition of an output transducer first, then ask what a thermistor does to its surroundings and what its surroundings do to it. Using the correct definition in each direction is what earns the top mark.

items: $S$ is 1 only when exactly one of $A$ and $B$ is 1 (the exclusive-OR function), and $C$ is 1 only when both are 1 (the AND function):

content.text: A thermistor's resistance depends on its temperature, so a change in the environment becomes an electrical quantity and it is an input transducer. When a voltage is applied it dissipates power, heats up and changes its surroundings, so it is also an output transducer.

Part (i). The upper AND gate receives $A$ together with $\overline{B}$, and the middle AND gate receives $\overline{A}$ together with $B$. The OR gate combines them, so $S = A\overline{B} + \overline{A}B$, which is the exclusive-OR function: it is 1 exactly when the two inputs differ. The lower AND gate receives $A$ and $B$ directly, so $C = A \cdot B$.

Part (ii). An input transducer converts a feature of the environment into an electrical parameter, whereas an output transducer converts an electrical parameter into a feature of the environment. A thermistor is a resistor whose resistance depends on its temperature, so when it is placed in the environment its resistance - an electrical quantity - responds to the temperature, and it is an input transducer. Connected to a voltage or current source it behaves as an ordinary resistor, dissipating power $P = VI$ and heating up, which changes the temperature of its surroundings; it is then an output transducer. The same device is therefore both.

content.text: Operational amplifiers

Part (i): identify each resistor by where it connects rather than by its value. One pair sets the gain of the first amplifier; look for the pair that is connected across the two supply rails and so sets a fixed potential instead.

Part (ii) has two separate calculations and you should do them in order. First the closed-loop gain of the first stage from the ratio of its two resistors. Then the potential that the divider puts on the second stage's inverting input, keeping the $15\,\mathrm{V}$ and $-15\,\mathrm{V}$ rails and the $18\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $12\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors straight.

With those two numbers, the second stage is a comparator. Draw the first output, then mark on it the value at which it crosses the reference potential - that crossing is where the square wave must switch, and it happens twice in every cycle of the input.

items: The $1.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and the left-hand $12\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors are the input and feedback resistors of the inverting amplifier X; the right-hand $12\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $18\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors form a potential divider that sets a fixed reference potential for Y.

$X_{out} = -8\,X_{in}$, an inverted triangular wave reaching $+8\,\mathrm{V}$ and $-8\,\mathrm{V}$. $Y_{out}$ is a square wave that switches between $+16\,\mathrm{V}$ and $-16\,\mathrm{V}$ whenever $X_{out}$ crosses the $-3.0\,\mathrm{V}$ reference, that is when $X_{in} = +0.375\,\mathrm{V}$.

content.text: Part (i). Amplifier X has its non-inverting input grounded, the input signal applied to the inverting input through $1.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, and negative feedback from its output to the same node through the left-hand $12\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor. Those two resistors are therefore the input resistor and the feedback resistor of an inverting amplifier. The right-hand $12\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $18\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors are in series between $+15\,\mathrm{V}$ and $-15\,\mathrm{V}$ and nothing else is connected to their junction, so they are a potential divider producing the fixed reference potential $Y_{in}$.

content.text: Outline similarities and differences between transistors and integrated circuits.
Write down what the two have in common first - how each is manufactured, and what has to be provided to keep either of them safe - and only then move on to the differences.
For the differences, ask how many transistors are contained in the device, how many electrical connections it has, and what sort of circuit each is normally used for.
A similarity has to be true of both, and a difference has to be true of one and not the other. Test each of your statements that way before you write it down.

Both are mass-produced by etching or diffusion on silicon chips and both need cooling; ICs contain many transistors on one chip, have many more connections, and suit low-power or complex circuits, while individual transistors remain used for high-power or simple circuits.

ICs and transistors are both mass-produced by etching/diffusion methods on silicon chips. ICs contain many transistors usually with other components on a single chip. Transistors have three connections but ICs usually have many more. Transistors are still individually used for high power or simple circuits whereas ICs are used for low power or complex circuits. Both require cooling arrangements and/or protective circuitry to prevent thermal damage.

content.text: Justify the use of LEDs over traditional forms of illumination in everyday situations.
The verb here is 'justify', so every advantage must be argued rather than merely listed. Pair each feature of an LED with the loss it causes in the alternative.
Think about where the energy goes in each lamp: how much is converted into light and how much into heat, and what that means for running costs and for the temperature of the fitting.

A fair justification has to acknowledge where LEDs are the worse option as well, such as their purchase cost and their restricted operating conditions. Leaving the counter-argument out costs marks at the top band.

LEDs give a single colour at any current with little heat loss, are available in all spectrum colours, respond fast and last longer, so they are more efficient, though they cost more and have restricted operating conditions.

While a modern LED produces a single frequency colour at any operating current with little heat loss, traditional forms of illumination such as an incandescent lamp have a maximum colour that is current dependent and loses considerable energy as heat loss. Modern LEDs are available in all spectrum colours while incandescent lamps need to be filtered to achieve a single colour, greatly increasing energy loss.

Originally the low light output of LEDs limited their use to small displays only, but modern ones can now be used for general illumination with high efficiency and long lifetimes compared to incandescent lamps. They can be used to form TV screens etc owing to their very fast response, but against this are their relatively higher cost and restricted temperature and operating conditions compared to other types of lighting.

content.text: Explain how the development of the silicon chip has influenced the development of electronics.
Chain your reasoning rather than listing benefits: a change in the chip produces a change in the device, which produces a change in what people are able to do. Follow each link explicitly.

The physical changes worth naming are how many components can be printed onto one crystal of silicon, how close together those components can be placed, and how small and how fast each individual element can be made.
Then state what those physical changes let engineers build, and finish by saying where the trend is now running out of room and what has to take over.

Printing thousands of components on one crystal of silicon has made devices smaller, cheaper, faster and lower in power, which has made computers, telephones and real-time audio and video portable and multi-functional.

Silicon chip technology allows semiconductor devices to be made on a single crystal layer of silicon. The ability to 'print' thousands of circuit elements rather than individual small diodes and transistors has significantly reduced the size and cost of electronic devices. Since switching is much quicker, owing to the close proximity of relevant components both within and between silicon chips, speed and memory have greatly increased with decreasing power consumption. The combining of once separate integrated circuits into single chips that perform different functions has facilitated the development of complex and multi-function devices. This has enabled equipment such as telephones and computers to become lightweight, compact and portable, and allowed the real-time capture and processing of audio and video images, and gaming and television capabilities.

The silicon chip has revolutionised the development of electronics and enabled complex processors and circuitry to be incorporated into everyday home appliances. As the size and speed of circuit elements has now approached a limiting atomic level, further developments in performance will come from development of multiple or parallel processing within silicon chips.
